title: Well-being measurement is becoming a policy-coordination technology, while Slovakia shows mixed progress and persistent trust, housing and education gaps
source_unit: OECD, Conceptualising and assessing well-being in the Slovak Republic: Building policy coherence for sustainable development
geography: Slovak Republic, with OECD, UNECE, SDG and peer-country framework comparison

observations.period: 2026 technical report; sustainable well-being measurement and policy application

denominator.unit: OECD technical report and comparative measurement-framework synthesis

framework_principles.value: Well-being frameworks distinguish current outcomes from their distribution and resources for future well-being; treat well-being as multidimensional; and combine objective and subjective measures.

current_dimensions.value: Common dimensions include subjective well-being, material conditions, work and leisure, housing, health, knowledge and skills, safety, social connections, civic engagement and environmental conditions; national frameworks may add culture, language, diversity, sports, preparedness and collective community well-being.

dashboard_choice.value: Most national and international initiatives use dashboards rather than a single composite index, with composite indices sometimes used as communication tools.

observations.method: OECD synthesis of international and national well-being frameworks, measurement guidance, policy applications and Slovak institutional planning.
observations.uncertainty: Framework recommendations describe measurement architecture and policy intent, not guaranteed adoption, causal policy effects or comparable lived outcomes across countries.
observations.subgroup: National statistical offices, ministries, policy evaluators, budget authorities and populations represented through official well-being indicators.
observations.counterinterpretation: A larger dashboard can create reporting burden, indicator conflict or symbolic measurement without changing budget decisions; a composite index can improve communication while hiding distributional trade-offs.

observations.period: Slovak Republic, 2010-2024 or latest available year; multidimensional well-being trend

denominator.unit: Slovak Republic indicator profile synthesized by OECD

improving_domains.value: Improvements are reported in income inequality, household wealth, difficulty making ends meet, life satisfaction, premature mortality, gender wage gap and gender parity in politics.

persistent_or_worsening_domains.value: Educational outcomes declined; housing affordability and overcrowding remain challenges; relative income poverty and household debt increased; trust in government deteriorated from already low levels.

mixed_progress.value: Material and selected quality-of-life indicators can improve while education, housing, poverty, debt and institutional trust move in less favorable directions.

observations.method: OECD Well-being Framework analysis of Slovak official and internationally comparable indicators, with trend thresholds and coverage review.
observations.uncertainty: The report combines indicators with different reference years and data sources; directional change does not establish a common cause or imply that all groups experienced the national trend equally.
observations.subgroup: Slovak residents differentiated by age, education and gender in the report's inequality analysis, alongside national material, quality-of-life and community-relations indicators.
observations.counterinterpretation: Aggregate improvements may coexist with concentrated hardship, and deteriorating trust may reflect political or information dynamics not captured by material indicators.

observations.period: 2026 report; well-being evidence entering government coordination and budgeting

denominator.unit: Slovak sustainable well-being framework and institutional implementation process

institutional_leadership.value: The Deputy Prime Minister's office, Government Office, Statistical Office and relevant ministries and stakeholders are developing a sustainable well-being framework and indicator dashboard linked to SDG implementation.

policy_uses.value: The report identifies strategic planning, policy appraisal, evaluation, performance management, budgeting and whole-of-government coordination as potential applications.

tradeoff_visibility.value: A well-being lens makes cross-sector interlinkages, synergies and trade-offs more explicit across economic, social and environmental objectives.

observations.method: Review of Slovak institutional arrangements and comparative OECD country practices, including national performance and budgeting examples.
observations.uncertainty: Identified applications are implementation pathways and institutional plans, not evidence that indicators already determine Slovak budget allocations or improve outcomes.
observations.subgroup: Government coordination bodies, statistical producers, ministries, budget authorities, stakeholders and communities affected by cross-sector policy trade-offs.
observations.counterinterpretation: Measurement can remain advisory if decision rights, budget rules, accountability and political incentives are not connected to the dashboard.

observations.period: 2026 report; data quality, disaggregation and future-well-being capacity

denominator.unit: OECD assessment of Slovak well-being data coverage and framework alignment

indicator_quality_criteria.value: Recommended criteria include timeliness, frequency, credibility, compatibility, accuracy, relevance, clear directional meaning, universality, measurability, disaggregation and understandability.

data_gaps.value: The report identifies gaps in official data coverage, timeliness and alignment with the OECD Well-being Framework.

future_resources.value: Sustainability is assessed through resources and capital stocks for future well-being, including natural, economic, human and social capital, separately from current outcomes.

observations.method: OECD data-availability review and framework alignment assessment, including current well-being, inequalities and resources for future well-being.
observations.uncertainty: Data availability and indicator quality vary by domain; missingness and non-comparable measures can make vulnerable groups and long-term degradation less visible.
observations.subgroup: Groups requiring disaggregation by age, education, gender, income and other relevant characteristics, plus future generations represented through sustainability-capital measures.
observations.counterinterpretation: More disaggregation is not automatically more useful if it compromises privacy, statistical reliability or institutional capacity to act on the evidence.

related_sources.claim: Official OECD publication page with abstract, date, metadata and downloadable report.
Related UN Beyond GDP agenda and 2026 expert-group implementation context.

boundary: This record adds an institutional measurement-and-policy layer: well-being dashboards are becoming a way to coordinate economic, social and environmental decisions, expose distributional and intergenerational trade-offs, and connect evidence to budgeting and strategy. It is a technical country report and comparative framework synthesis, not respondent-level ingestion, a causal evaluation of dashboard use, a complete national welfare account or proof that measurement changes policy.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The official OECD publication page and 73-page PDF were reviewed for framework principles, dimensions, dashboard design, Slovak trends, institutional arrangements, policy applications, data gaps, disaggregation and sustainability-capital boundaries.
